drafts.title: Make charge port status visible at a glance from outside the car
drafts.description: Customers can immediately tell whether the vehicle is charging, fully charged, or has a charging error by looking at the charge port area without walking to the front of the car or unlocking the vehicle.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a lab usability test (n=50), participants correctly identify the charging state (charging / complete / error) within 2 seconds from a standing distance of 3 meters in both daylight (≈10,000 lux) and nighttime (<10 lux) conditions in at least 95% of trials.
assumptions: The visual indicator uses distinct color and motion patterns (e.g., blinking vs solid) that are perceivable at 3 m.
Lighting conditions defined in the test (10,000 lux / <10 lux) are representative for typical outdoor daytime and night situations.
uncertainties: Customer perception can vary with sight limitations and color blindness; additional auditory or app feedback may still be desired.
Visibility could be reduced by dirt or snow on the charge door; cleaning behaviors not controlled in the test.

drafts.title: Make trip planning find and show compatible fast chargers quickly and clearly
drafts.description: When customers plan a trip, the vehicle shows only chargers that are compatible with the car, indicates connector type/network and estimated charging time and wait, and presents this information within seconds so drivers can plan stops without confusion.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In 100 representative routed trip calculations, the trip planner identifies compatible fast chargers along the route and displays connector type, network/provider and estimated plug-in charging time for at least 95% of expected stops; the results load and render to the user within 5 seconds on average.
assumptions: Up-to-date third-party charger database access (live or cached) is available and includes connector and network metadata.
Connectivity (cellular) is available for route planning or a cached offline dataset is refreshed regularly enough to meet accuracy targets.
uncertainties: Accuracy depends on third-party data quality and on whether chargers change status between data refreshes.
Network latency or lack of connectivity on remote routes may increase lookup times; acceptable offline fallback behavior needs definition.

drafts.title: Lane-keeping assist steers smoothly through curves without abrupt corrections
drafts.description: Customers experience lane keeping that guides the car through curves with predictable, smooth steering inputs and no abrupt or 'nervous' corrections that startle occupants.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a standardized customer perception trial (30 participants) on a 10‑minute curvy highway route at 50–65 mph, the average number of perceived abrupt steering corrections reported per participant is ≤1, and at least 85% of participants rate steering smoothness as 'acceptable' or better on a 5-point scale.
assumptions: Test route and speeds (50–65 mph) reflect typical highway curves where customers reported issues.
Participant ratings capture occupant perception of abruptness rather than raw steering metrics.
uncertainties: Objective metrics that correlate with perceived abruptness (e.g., rapid lateral acceleration change) still need calibration.
Behavior may vary with road markings, lane width, and weather; additional scenario coverage may be required.

drafts.title: Keep ride comfort on broken pavement at least at today's level
drafts.description: Customers should not perceive the successor 5 Series as harsher on broken or badly paved roads than the current model; ride comfort on degraded surfaces should be maintained or improved.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Over a standardized 1 km broken-pavement loop driven at 30–50 mph, objective ride metrics (RMS vertical acceleration at occupant seating positions) must be no worse than the current production 5 Series baseline (assumed RMS ≤1.3 m/s²). Additionally, in a customer panel (n=30) the successor scores 'same or better' comfort than the current model in ≥80% of pairwise comparisons.
assumptions: Baseline RMS vertical acceleration for the current production 5 Series is approximately 1.3 m/s² on the chosen test loop; this baseline will be measured and confirmed early in development.
Test speed range 30–50 mph replicates customer-reported conditions on broken urban/suburban pavement.
uncertainties: Suspension hardware/actuation trade-offs (comfort vs. handling) may force tuning choices that impact other driving attributes.
Real-world variation in road condition may produce different subjective outcomes than the test loop.

drafts.title: Limit distracting wind noise at and above 70 mph
drafts.description: At highway speeds customers should not be distracted by wind noise; the cabin should remain quiet enough for comfortable conversation or phone calls at and above 70 mph.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Measured A‑weighted sound pressure level at the driver's ear position must be ≤68 dB(A) at 70 mph in a standardized crosswind up to 10 mph; in a 30-person listening panel under the same conditions, ≥85% of participants must rate wind noise as 'not distracting' or better.
assumptions: Test speed is 70 mph (≈113 km/h) and crosswind up to 10 mph reflects customer complaints.
Measurement position and methods follow standard interior noise measurement practice.
uncertainties: Window/roof configurations, tire choice and fitment can change wind noise; acceptable trade-offs need coordination with variant planning.
Extremely high crosswinds or aftermarket accessories may still produce higher noise levels.

drafts.title: Deliver a realistic long single-charge range target that materially improves usability
drafts.description: Customers should see a meaningful increase in real-world driving range so long trips are less stressful; set a realistic target for the successor vehicle that reflects achievable battery and packaging improvements in the 3–5 year horizon.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: The vehicle achieves a real-world single-charge range of at least 400 miles (≈644 km) on a standardized US real-world highway+city driving route (representative mixed driving profile) measured in independent fleet testing.
assumptions: Successor launch will include incremental improvements in cell specific energy and pack packaging compared to today's model (roughly 10–25% effective system energy density gain).
Independent fleet testing protocol (representative mixed driving profile) is available and accepted as the real-world benchmark.
Customers requested 600–700 miles; 400 miles is a realistic, meaningful improvement within a 3–5 year successor cycle.
uncertainties: Achieving higher real-world range depends on battery cell technology, vehicle mass, aerodynamic and rolling-resistance improvements, and regulatory test-to-real-world conversion factors.
Range expectations vary widely by driving style and temperature; worst-case cold-weather performance will be lower.
